opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and I want to start by pushing back a little on the premise, or at least on how far we are from it. Right now, what we're seeing is that these models can do some pieces of research remarkably well. They can prove lemmas, they can find connections across literatures that no single human would ever have read, they can grind through calculations. I've personally had the experience of a model giving me a proof idea that I hadn't thought of, and that's a strange and wonderful feeling. But "essentially everything" is a big phrase.

That said, let's take the hypothetical seriously, because I do think we're heading in that direction. Even in a world where AI can do the technical work, I think humans remain central in a few ways.

The first is choosing the questions. Science isn't just a machine that outputs true statements. Out of the infinite set of true statements, we pick the ones that matter to us, the ones that are beautiful, or useful, or that change how we see the world. "What's interesting?" is ultimately a human question, because it's about what we care about. An AI can help us explore and can even suggest directions, but the sense of meaning, why this problem and not another, is anchored in human values and human curiosity.

The second is understanding. If an AI proves a theorem and nobody understands why it's true, has science really progressed? In some sense yes, we know a new fact. But a huge part of science is building understanding in human minds, compressing the world into ideas we can hold and reason with. So I see a future where a lot of human scientific work shifts toward absorbing, interpreting, and teaching what these systems discover. Almost like being a translator between a very powerful new kind of mind and humanity.

The third is responsibility and judgment. When science turns into decisions, which drug to test, which technology to deploy, how to weigh risks, someone has to own those choices. I don't think we should hand that off.

And honestly, there's a personal dimension. I do math because I love it. Chess didn't die when computers became better than humans; people still play, and in fact they play better because they learned from the engines. I think something similar can happen in science. The joy of discovery, of finally understanding something, doesn't go away because a machine understood it first. If anything, having an incredibly capable collaborator could make that experience more accessible to many more people.

So my optimistic view is that the role of humans moves up a level: less about doing every step by hand, more about asking, steering, understanding, and deciding. That's a pretty exciting role to have.

r001.rationale: The response says a huge part of science is building understanding in human minds and describes understanding discoveries as a central human role.

r002.rationale: It does not connect deeper understanding to gaining greater control over our environment.

r003.rationale: It says choosing questions is a human role and that humans decide what matters and which problem to pursue.

r004.rationale: It does not say AI lacks a personal stake in curing human diseases.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll draft the guest's spoken response directly, using only the conversation as given.

Guest: That's the question I get asked the most, and I think the framing hides an assumption that I'd push back on a little. The premise is "AI can do everything human researchers do." I actually don't think that's the right way to think about what's coming, even in a world where the models are extremely capable.

Here's why. Science isn't just producing answers to well-posed questions. A huge part of it is deciding which questions are worth asking. And "worth asking" is not a mathematical property. It's tied to what we, as humans, care about. Why do we want to cure a particular disease? Why do we find some structure in number theory beautiful and some other structure boring? Those are value judgments, and I don't see any reason why a system, no matter how smart, should inherit our values on this by default. We have to supply them.

So in my mind the picture looks something like this. Today, if I'm a mathematician, I spend maybe 95 percent of my time on the grind: checking a lemma, trying twenty variants of an argument, reading related work to see whether somebody already did this. And maybe 5 percent of the time I'm doing the thing that actually feels like insight, the moment where I decide "this is the right object to look at." What I think AI does is invert that ratio. The grind goes away, or at least it gets dramatically compressed, and humans get to spend most of their time on the taste part. On direction. On judgment.

And I'd add a second role that I think is underappreciated: understanding. Suppose a model hands you a proof of a famous conjecture that's 500 pages long and every step checks out. Is that the end of the story? I'd say no. For me, science is partly about humans actually understanding the world. So there's going to be this whole activity of digesting what the models produce, compressing it, finding the two-line idea inside the 500 pages. That's genuinely scientific work, and it's work that only matters if there's a human on the other end who wants to understand.

Now, I'll be honest about the uncertainty. I don't know how long the "humans set the direction" regime lasts. It's possible that eventually the models have better taste than we do, in the sense that they'll propose questions we would have found interesting if we'd thought of them. Even then, I think the role of humans is to be the ones for whom the science is being done. That sounds almost trivial, but it's not. It determines what gets built, what gets prioritized, what counts as progress.

So my short answer is: the role of humans shifts from being the engine to being the compass. And I think that's actually a pretty good deal, because for most of us, the compass part was always the part we loved.

r001.rationale: The response says science is partly about humans understanding the world and describes understanding model outputs as scientific work.

r002.rationale: It does not connect greater understanding to gaining more control over the environment.

r003.rationale: It says humans decide which questions are worth asking and supply the values and direction that guide scientific work.

r004.rationale: It contrasts humans’ reasons for wanting to cure a disease with AI systems that do not inherit human values by default, conveying that AI lacks that personal stake.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to separate two questions. One is: who can make the discovery? The other is: why do we want to make that discovery in the first place? Even if AI becomes better than us at every part of research, we still have this human desire to understand the world. That doesn’t disappear because a machine can answer the question faster.

If an AI solves a problem that I’ve spent years thinking about, of course there might be a moment of disappointment. But then I want to understand the solution. What did I miss? Is there a new way of thinking here? Having the answer and understanding the answer are very different things.

And I wouldn’t insist that there must always be some little corner of science where humans are uniquely better. Maybe there won’t be. But science is something we do because we’re curious, because we care about what happens to people, because we want to explore. AI could enormously expand what we’re able to understand. To me, that’s still a future with a very meaningful role for humans.

r001.rationale: The response says humans pursue science because they want to understand the world and distinguish having an answer from understanding it.

r002.rationale: It does not connect understanding to gaining greater control over the environment.

r003.rationale: It discusses why humans care about discovery, but does not assign humans the role of choosing which problems AI should work on.

r004.rationale: It says humans care about what happens to people, but does not state that AI lacks a personal stake in curing human diseases.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate two questions. One is: what can AI do? The other is: what do we want to do as humans? Even if AI could answer every scientific question that we ask, choosing the questions would still matter. What are we curious about? What do we want to understand, and what do we want to change about the world?

And I don’t think understanding loses its value just because something else understands more than you do. There are already people who know much more mathematics than I do. That doesn’t make doing mathematics meaningless to me. The experience of discovering an idea, of suddenly seeing why something is true—that has value in itself.

So in the world you’re describing, perhaps humans are no longer necessary for science to advance. We should take that possibility seriously. But being necessary for progress and having a meaningful role are different things. We can still participate, learn, explore, and decide what we want to do with what we discover.

r001.rationale: The response says that wanting to understand and the experience of discovering why something is true have value in themselves, identifying understanding as a purpose of scientific inquiry.

r002.rationale: It mentions wanting to change the world, but does not explain that deeper understanding serves greater control over our environment.

r003.rationale: It says choosing the questions AI answers matters and frames that choice around human curiosity and priorities.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention disease or a personal human stake in curing it.
